questions.prompt: Which of the following is an example of wealth rather than income for a household in Veld?
hints: Use the difference between a stock of assets and a flow of money received.
For each option, ask whether it is something owned at a point in time or something received over a period.

options.text: The monthly salary earned by one of the parents
options.misconception: A salary is a flow of money received from work, which is income.

options.text: The dividends received each year from shares
options.misconception: Dividends are a flow of payments from owning shares, so they count as income.

options.text: The house that the family owns
The pension paid each month to a grandparent
options.misconception: A pension is a regular payment received, which is income.

questions.prompt: Which statement is about equity rather than equality?
hints: Equity involves a judgement, while equality can be measured.
Look for the statement that people could disagree with because it depends on values rather than data.

options.text: It is unfair that the richest 10% of Veld's households receive half of all income
The richest 10% of Veld's households receive half of all income
options.misconception: This is a factual statement about how income is shared, so it concerns equality.

options.text: Each quintile of Kuva's population receives 20% of total income
options.misconception: This describes a perfectly equal distribution, which is a measurable fact.

options.text: Veld's Gini coefficient rose from 0.35 to 0.40 over ten years
options.misconception: A change in a measure of distribution is a positive statement about equality.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between income and wealth.
hints: One is measured over a period of time and the other at a point in time.
For each, say what it consists of and give a short example.
marking_points: Income is the flow of money received over a period of time, e.g. wages, interest, rent, dividends or transfer payments [1]
Wealth is the stock of assets owned at a point in time, e.g. savings, shares, bonds, land or houses [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer identifies income as a flow received over time and wealth as a stock of assets owned, each with an example.

questions.prompt: Over ten years, Kuva's Lorenz curve moves further away from the line of perfect equality. What does this show?
hints: Think about the area between the line of equality and the Lorenz curve.
Decide what happens to that area when the curve moves outward, then link the area to the Gini coefficient.
questions.targets: Direction of Lorenz shift and Gini change

options.text: The Gini coefficient fell and income inequality decreased
options.misconception: A curve closer to the line of equality would show this, not one moving away.

options.text: The Gini coefficient rose and income inequality increased
The Gini coefficient rose and income inequality decreased
options.misconception: A higher Gini coefficient always means more, not less, inequality.

options.text: Average income in Kuva fell
options.misconception: A Lorenz curve shows shares of income, not the level of average income.

questions.prompt: Define the term Gini coefficient.
hints: Your definition should refer to the Lorenz curve diagram.
Mention how the measure is calculated from the diagram and the range of values it can take.
questions.targets: Gini as a ratio of areas
marking_points: A measure of income inequality calculated as the area between the line of equality and the Lorenz curve divided by the total area under the line of equality [1]
It ranges from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (perfect inequality) [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer gives the ratio of areas from the Lorenz curve diagram and the range from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (perfect inequality).

questions.prompt: Using Table 1, what share of total income is received by the poorest 60% of Kuva's households?
hints: The poorest 60% of households is made up of more than one quintile.
Add the income shares of the quintiles, starting from the poorest, until you cover 60% of households.
questions.targets: Cumulative income shares for a Lorenz curve

table.caption: Table 1: Share of total income by quintile in Kuva

options.misconception: This is the share of the third quintile only, not the cumulative share.
This is the share of the population, not the share of income it receives.
This is the share received by the poorest 80% of households.

questions.prompt: Using Table 2, calculate the cumulative share of income that would be plotted for each quintile on Veld's Lorenz curve. State the share of income received by the poorest 60% of households.
hints: A Lorenz curve plots cumulative shares of population against cumulative shares of income.
Start with the poorest quintile and keep adding the next quintile's share until you reach the richest.
questions.targets: Building a Lorenz curve from quintile data

table.caption: Table 2: Share of total income by quintile in Veld

marking_points: Shares are added cumulatively from the poorest quintile, e.g. 6 + 11 = 17 [1]
Cumulative shares: 6%, 17%, 33%, 55%, 100% [1]
The poorest 60% of households receive 33% of income [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer shows the cumulative addition, gives all five cumulative figures and states 33% for the poorest 60%.

questions.prompt: Using Table 3, which country has the most unequal distribution of income?
hints: Recall what a Gini coefficient close to 0 and close to 1 means.
Compare the four coefficients and link the size of each to how far its Lorenz curve would lie from the line of equality.

options.text: Veld
options.misconception: A lower Gini coefficient means a more equal distribution, not a less equal one.

options.text: Kuva
options.misconception: Kuva is fairly unequal, but another country has a higher coefficient.

options.text: Tarn
options.misconception: Tarn is in the middle of the range.

options.text: Oska

questions.prompt: Table 4 shows that Kuva's Gini coefficient changed between 2015 and 2025. Explain how this change would be shown on a Lorenz curve diagram and what it means for income distribution.
hints: Use a Lorenz curve diagram with the line of perfect equality.
Link the direction of the Gini change to the area between the two lines, then to the position of the curve.
questions.targets: Gini change shown as Lorenz shift
marking_points: The Lorenz curve for 2025 lies closer to the line of perfect equality than the 2015 curve [1]
The area between the line of equality and the Lorenz curve is smaller, so the Gini coefficient falls from 0.42 to 0.35 [1]
Income is more equally distributed / income inequality has fallen [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer describes the Lorenz curve moving towards the line of equality, links the smaller area to the lower Gini coefficient and concludes that inequality fell.

questions.prompt: A household in Veld earns less than half of the median household income, but it can still afford enough food, housing and clothing to meet its basic needs. This household is:
hints: Check each part of the scenario against the two types of poverty.
One type compares income with other people in society; the other asks whether basic needs can be met.

options.text: in relative poverty but not in absolute poverty
in absolute poverty but not in relative poverty
options.misconception: Absolute poverty means basic needs cannot be met, but this household can meet them.

options.text: in both absolute and relative poverty
options.misconception: Being able to meet basic needs rules out absolute poverty.

options.text: in neither absolute nor relative poverty
options.misconception: Income below half the median is a common threshold for relative poverty.

questions.prompt: Define the term relative poverty.
hints: Your definition should say what a household's income is compared with.
Include the kind of threshold that is commonly used.
marking_points: A situation where a household's income is low compared with other households in the same society [1]
Usually measured as income below a set percentage (e.g. 50% or 60%) of median income [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer compares income with the rest of society and refers to a threshold based on median income.

questions.prompt: The Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) measures poverty using which three dimensions?
hints: The MPI looks at deprivations rather than at money income.
Think of the non-income areas of life that the index checks at household level.

options.text: Income, wealth and consumption
options.misconception: These are monetary measures, but the MPI was designed to look beyond income.

options.text: Health, education and living standards
Employment, income and housing
options.misconception: Employment and income are not among the MPI's three dimensions.

options.text: Income per capita, life expectancy and literacy
options.misconception: This is close to the Human Development Index, which includes income per capita.

questions.prompt: In Kuva, median household income is 30,000 kuvan dollars and the relative poverty line is set at 60% of median income. Using Table 5, which household is in relative poverty?
hints: Work out the relative poverty line first using the median.
Compare each household's income with that line, not with the median itself.

table.caption: Table 5: Annual income of selected households in Kuva

options.text: Household X
options.misconception: This household's income is below two-thirds of the median, but not below 60% of it.

options.text: Household Y
options.misconception: This household's income is below the median, but well above the poverty line.

options.text: Household W
Household Z
options.misconception: Having an income just below the median does not mean being in relative poverty.

questions.prompt: In Veld, median household income is 24,000 zed and the relative poverty line is 50% of median income. Using Table 6, calculate the relative poverty line and the percentage of these households that are in relative poverty.
hints: Apply the given percentage to the median income to find the line.
Compare each household with the line, count those below it and express the count as a percentage of all five households.

table.caption: Table 6: Annual income of five households in Veld

marking_points: Relative poverty line = 50% × 24,000 = 12,000 zed [1]
Households A, C and E have incomes below 12,000 zed [1]
3 / 5 × 100 = 60% of the households are in relative poverty [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer finds the 12,000 zed line, identifies households A, C and E, and gives 60%.

questions.prompt: Explain why the Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) may give a more complete picture of poverty in Kuva than a measure based only on income.
hints: Compare what an income measure captures with what the MPI captures.
Think of a household with income above a poverty line that still lacks something important, and link this to the MPI's dimensions.
marking_points: Income measures only show whether money income is below a threshold [1]
The MPI measures deprivations in health, education and living standards (e.g. nutrition, schooling, clean water, electricity) [1]
So it can identify households that are poor in ways income does not show, e.g. lacking access to schools or clean water despite some income [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer contrasts the single income measure with the MPI's three dimensions and explains how the MPI reveals hidden deprivation.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an example of inequality of opportunity in Veld?
hints: Inequality of opportunity is about circumstances, not choices or results.
For each option, ask whether the person could have controlled the cause of the difference.

options.text: Children born in remote villages have no access to a secondary school
Two equally skilled workers earn different amounts because one chooses to work part-time
options.misconception: This difference comes from a personal choice, not from circumstances beyond the worker's control.

options.text: A successful entrepreneur earns more than an employee in the same industry
options.misconception: A difference in outcomes is not by itself a difference in opportunity.

options.text: Doctors earn more than shop assistants
options.misconception: A pay gap between occupations describes unequal outcomes, not unequal opportunities.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is most likely to widen income inequality in Kuva?
hints: Think about which groups gain and which lose from each change.
Pick the change that increases incomes at the top more than at the bottom.

options.text: An expansion of free, high-quality public education
options.misconception: Wider access to education usually narrows skill gaps and reduces inequality.

options.text: A rise in the minimum wage for low-paid workers
options.misconception: A higher minimum wage raises incomes at the bottom of the distribution.

options.text: Technological change that raises demand for highly skilled workers only
An increase in unemployment benefits
options.misconception: Higher benefits raise the incomes of the poorest households.

questions.prompt: Explain how inequality of opportunity can lead to income inequality in Veld. Use an example in your answer.
hints: Start with a circumstance a person cannot control, such as where they are born.
Link that circumstance to human capital, then to the jobs and income the person can obtain.
questions.targets: Opportunity to human capital to income chain
marking_points: Some people face circumstances beyond their control, e.g. being born in a poor rural area with weak schools or health care [1]
They build less human capital (fewer skills, less education, poorer health) [1]
So they are more likely to end up in low-paid jobs or unemployed, widening the gap in incomes [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer gives a relevant example of unequal circumstances and links it through human capital to lower earnings.

questions.prompt: Explain how globalization and technological change may widen income inequality within Kuva.
hints: Consider which workers gain and which workers lose when trade expands and new technology is adopted.
Make one link for globalization and one for technology, each ending with an effect on relative incomes.
marking_points: Globalization lets firms move low-skilled production to lower-wage countries / face more import competition [1]
So demand for, and wages of, low-skilled workers in Kuva fall, while firms and skilled workers gain from larger markets [1]
Technological change automates routine jobs and raises demand for highly skilled workers [1]
So wages of skilled workers rise relative to low-skilled workers, widening the income gap [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer explains both causes, each linked to a change in the relative wages of skilled and low-skilled workers.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a likely consequence of very high income inequality in Veld?
hints: Think about how income affects a family's ability to invest in its children.
Link that investment to the chances children have of moving up the income ladder.

options.text: Faster growth in consumption, because richer households spend a larger share of their income
options.misconception: Richer households usually spend a smaller share of their income, not a larger one.

options.text: Lower social mobility, as low-income families cannot afford to invest in education and health
A fall in relative poverty
options.misconception: High inequality usually means more households fall well below median income.

options.text: More equal access to health care
options.misconception: Unequal incomes tend to create unequal access to services that must be paid for.

questions.prompt: Explain two ways in which high income inequality may reduce economic growth in Kuva.
hints: Consider effects on spending and effects on human capital.
For each way, state the effect and then link it to real GDP or potential output.
marking_points: Way 1, e.g. low-income households cannot afford education and health care [1]
Explained, e.g. human capital is lower than it could be, reducing productivity and potential output [1]
Way 2, e.g. income is concentrated among the rich, who spend a smaller share of it / social and political tension rises [1]
Explained, e.g. consumption and AD grow more slowly, or instability discourages investment, slowing growth [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer gives two distinct mechanisms, each linked clearly to lower output or slower growth.

questions.prompt: Explain how wealth inequality in Veld can make income inequality larger over time.
hints: Think about the types of income that wealth can generate.
Follow what happens when that income is saved or passed on across generations.
marking_points: Wealth generates income in the form of interest, dividends and rent [1]
Wealthy households can save and reinvest this income, adding to their wealth and future income [1]
Wealth can also be passed to the next generation, so the gap between rich and poor persists and widens [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer links wealth to property income, then to further accumulation or inheritance that widens the gap over time.

questions.prompt: Table 7 shows the income tax paid by three people in Kuva. Which type of tax is this?
hints: Classify taxes by the share of income paid, not by the amount paid.
Work out tax paid divided by income for each person and see how it changes as income rises.

table.caption: Table 7: Income and income tax paid in Kuva

options.text: A proportional tax
options.misconception: The share of income paid in tax is not constant across the three people.

options.text: A regressive tax
options.misconception: Higher-income people are not paying a smaller share of their income.

options.text: A lump-sum tax, because everyone pays a fixed amount
options.misconception: The amount paid differs from person to person.

options.text: A progressive tax

questions.prompt: Define the term progressive taxation.
hints: Your definition should compare taxpayers with different income levels.
Consider what happens to the tax burden as income rises, and how that burden is best measured.
marking_points: A tax where the proportion of income paid as tax [1]
increases as income increases / the average tax rate rises with income [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer refers to the percentage (not amount) of income paid in tax rising as income rises.

questions.prompt: Using the tax bands in Table 8, a worker in Veld has taxable income of 40,000 zed. What is the worker's average tax rate?
hints: Average tax rate = total tax paid ÷ total income × 100.
Apply each band's rate only to the part of income that falls inside that band, add these amounts, then divide by income.
questions.targets: Average vs marginal tax rate with bands

table.caption: Table 8: Income tax bands in Veld
columns: Tax rate on income in this band

options.misconception: This is the marginal tax rate on the last zed earned, not the average rate.
This averages the two positive band rates instead of dividing total tax by income.
This confuses the amount of tax paid, in thousands of zed, with a percentage.

questions.prompt: Using Table 9, a worker in Kuva has taxable income of 30,000 kuvan dollars. Calculate the total income tax paid, the worker's average tax rate and the worker's marginal tax rate.
hints: Apply each band's rate only to the income that falls inside that band.
Add the tax from each band, divide the total by income for the average rate, and look at the band of the last dollar earned for the marginal rate.
questions.targets: Band-by-band tax, average and marginal rates

table.caption: Table 9: Income tax bands in Kuva
columns: Tax rate on income in this band

marking_points: = 4,200 kuvan dollars [1]
Average tax rate = 4,200 / 30,000 × 100 = 14%; marginal tax rate = 30% [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer applies the rates band by band to reach 4,200 kuvan dollars, then gives an average rate of 14% and a marginal rate of 30%.

questions.prompt: Why do indirect taxes, such as a sales tax on food, tend to increase income inequality?
hints: Compare the tax paid with each household's income, not with the price of the good.
Think about what share of income poorer and richer households spend on everyday goods.

options.text: High-income households pay a larger amount of the tax, which discourages them from working
options.misconception: Indirect taxes are paid on spending, not on work, and paying a larger amount does not make a tax unequalizing.

options.text: Low-income households spend a larger share of their income on taxed goods, so the tax takes a larger share of their income
The tax rate on the good rises as the buyer's income rises
options.misconception: The rate on a good is the same for every buyer, whatever their income.

options.text: Indirect taxes are only paid by firms, which then cut the wages of low-paid workers
options.misconception: Much of an indirect tax is passed on to consumers through higher prices.

questions.prompt: Which policy is most likely to shift Veld's Lorenz curve towards the line of perfect equality?
hints: Look at both sides of each policy: who pays and who benefits.
Pick the policy whose overall effect raises the income share of the poorest relative to the richest.

options.text: Replacing a progressive income tax with a proportional income tax
options.misconception: A flat rate takes a smaller share from high earners than before, so inequality tends to rise.

options.text: Raising the sales tax on basic food items
options.misconception: A tax on basic goods takes a larger share of income from poorer households.

options.text: Raising the top marginal income tax rate and using the revenue to increase unemployment benefits
Cutting spending on public schools and hospitals in low-income areas
options.misconception: This reduces services that benefit poorer households most.

questions.prompt: Explain how a progressive income tax combined with transfer payments can reduce income inequality in Kuva. Refer to a Lorenz curve diagram in your answer.
hints: Think about which households each part of the policy affects most.
Link the change in disposable incomes to income shares, then describe the shift of the Lorenz curve and the change in the Gini coefficient.
questions.targets: Tax and transfers on the Lorenz curve
marking_points: A progressive tax takes a larger share of income from high-income earners [1]
Transfer payments (e.g. unemployment benefits, pensions) raise the disposable income of low-income households [1]
Disposable income becomes more evenly distributed, so the income share of the poorest rises [1]
The Lorenz curve shifts towards the line of perfect equality and the Gini coefficient falls [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer explains both parts of the policy and describes the Lorenz curve moving towards the line of equality with a lower Gini coefficient.

questions.prompt: The government of Veld plans a large rise in the top marginal income tax rate. Suggest two reasons why this may reduce income inequality by less than expected.
hints: Think about how high earners might respond to the change.
Consider effects on work, on where income is reported, and on the tax revenue actually collected.
marking_points: Reason 1, e.g. high earners may avoid or evade the tax, or move income or residence abroad, so less revenue is collected [1]
Reason 2, e.g. it may reduce incentives to work or invest, slowing growth and job creation that would help lower-income groups [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer gives two distinct, plausible reasons such as tax avoidance/capital flight and disincentive effects.
